result.final_text:
## What this letter says
This letter is from a clinic doctor. It is about your son Abc. He is 9 months old. He was born in a twin pregnancy. He was born a little early. The letter says this was very mild.

He has had wheezing, cough and shortness of breath for several months. He still has a cough. This is after treatment with inhaled steroids and a bronchodilator.

There is no smoke exposure. His father, uncle and older sister have asthma.

The parents live in separate homes. The letter says there is a question about how steadily his medicine is given at his father's house.

The doctor examined Abc. Some scattered rhonchi were heard. They cleared when he coughed. He was otherwise healthy.

The doctor thinks Abc probably has fairly severe childhood asthma. This is not certain. Luckily, he has not had to go to hospital.

The letter says his mother knows the basics of asthma care quite well.

## What you need to do
1. The letter says to continue his alternate day steroids. Continue until he has no symptoms at all on the days off steroids.
2. The letter says it would be reasonable to keep lowering (weaning) the dose. It can go down to as low as 1.5 milligrams (0.5 milliliters) on alternate days.
3. The letter says his mother is encouraged to contact the clinic office. Questions can be answered by phone if needed.

## Dates and medicines
The letter has no date.

- Inhaled steroids: dose and how often are not stated. He has a cough even with this.
- Bronchodilator: dose and how often are not stated. He has a cough even with this.
- Prednisolone, short burst: recently started. Dose and how often are not stated.
- Prednisolone, alternate day course: the dose is being lowered. The letter says it is reasonable to go down to as low as 1.5 milligrams (0.5 milliliters) on alternate days. His current dose is not stated.

## Questions to ask your doctor
- What dose of prednisolone is Abc taking now?
- What are the doses of the inhaled steroids and the bronchodilator?
- How will we know he has no symptoms on the days off steroids?

## When to get urgent help
The letter does not list specific warning signs.

If you are worried and it is not an emergency, call NHS 111. In an emergency, call 999.

---
*This explanation was made by a computer program to help you read your letter. It may contain mistakes. It does not replace your doctor, nurse or pharmacist. Always follow the letter and ask them if anything is unclear.*
